newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No salvage plan for nuclear waste at sea - Greenpeace.
newsitem.headline: No salvage plan for nuclear waste at sea - Greenpeace.

text.p: Nuclear-power nations have no plans to salvage any nuclear waste lost in the deep seas, according to a document released by the environmental group Greenpeace on Tuesday.

Greenpeace said the document, which it said was leaked from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), made a mockery of safety assurances made by London, Paris and Tokyo over a shipment of plutonium waste now on its way from France to Japan.
The British-registered ship Pacific Teal is currently believed to be south of Australia enroute from France to Japan with 40 blocks of reprocessed plutonium waste.

Greenpeace said leaked minutes from a November 1996 IAEA advisory group meeting on maritime transport of nuclear material revealed nuclear-power nations had no plans to salvage nuclear waste lost at sea.

"The issue of locating and identifying sunken ships or flasks and the need to salvage the ship or flasks is not only a technical, but it is also a political and economic issue," said the document, a copy of which Greenpeace issued to Reuters.
The document went on to say that "...sea recovery of lower radioactive material packages or of packages of any sort at greater depths (below 200 metres or 656 feet), was not justified".
"In general, most situations would lead to negligible harm to the environment and minimal exposure to man if the packages were not recovered following the accident," the document said.
However, the document did say that if highly toxic radioactive materials were lost on the continental shelf there would be "large exposures" of radioactivity.
"This certainly helps to explain why British, French and Japanese officials sought to keep secret the details of these transports," said Greenpeace International spokesman Damon Moglen in Sydney.
Greenpeace said all three countries had been represented at the November meeting of the IAEA advisory group.
"What is happening is that they don't even have (salvage) plans and they don't want to talk to people about this," Moglen told Reuters.

A number of nations along the Pacific Teal's route, such as New Zealand, Argentina, Portugal, Malaysia and the small South Pacific island countries have condemned the shipment of nuclear waste through their regions.

South Africa suggested earlier this month that it would take a tougher line on nuclear waste shipments past its coast after the Pacific Teal broke a promise not to sail inside the republic's 200-mile exclusive economic zone.
But Australia, which led a South Pacific campaign against French nuclear testing in the region, has avoided the controversy over the shipment, saying it is satisfied with safety assurances.

The Australian upper house Senate last week passed a motion calling on the government to make public the route of the Pacific Teal. But Australian Environment Minister Robert Hill told the Senate: "We do not feel, as a nation, threatened by the potential of any accident".
Greenpeace's Moglen said the environment group expected the Pacific Teal to sail through the Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand.
"The nuclear industry is using the route around the Cape of Good Hope and through the Tasman Sea because they hoped they could avoid public and political opposition," said Moglen.
The Pacific Teal nuclear waste shipment from France to Japan is among the first of about 30 planned.
